Block i is the product of the i consecutive integers ending at T(i) = i(i+1)/2, i.e., block i = T(i)! / (T(i)−i)!. F(n) sums blocks 1..n. With n ≤ 1000, the largest factorial index is T(1000) = 500500 — small enough to precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7, making each block an O(1) quotient. Alternatively, since n is tiny, directly simulating each block with modular multiplication (O(n²) ≈ 5·10⁵ multiplications) is perfectly fast and needs no number theory.

Example 1: blocks 1, 6, 120 sum to 127. Example 2: the seven blocks sum to 6006997207, reduced mod 1e9+7 to 6997165.
k: Block i = T(i)!/(T(i)−i)! with T(i) = i(i+1)/2
Modular division via Fermat: inv(x) = x^(MOD−2), precompute inverse factorials once
n ≤ 1000 makes even the naive O(n²) simulation fast

a.i: Maintain a running integer pointer num. For each block i, multiply i consecutive values starting at num into an accumulator (mod p), advancing num each time. Total work is 1+2+…+n = O(n²), trivial for n ≤ 1000.
s: For i from 1 to n: cur = 1; multiply cur by num, num++, i times, all mod 1e9+7
Add cur to ans mod 1e9+7; return ans
a.t: O(n²) — triangular number of modular multiplications (≈5·10⁵ for n=1000)

a.i: Recognize block i as a ratio of factorials at index T(i). Precompute factorials and inverse factorials (via Fermat's little theorem) up to T(n); each block then costs O(1), giving O(T(n)) overall — useful if n were much larger.
s: N = n(n+1)/2; build fact[0..N] and invfact[0..N] mod 1e9+7 (invfact[N] = pow(fact[N], MOD−2), then descend)
For each i, T = i(i+1)/2; block = fact[T] · invfact[T−i] mod p
a.t: O(n²) preprocessing for factorials (dominated by building tables of size T(n)), O(n) for the summation
a.sp: O(n²) — factorial tables of size T(n) ≈ 500500

w: For the given constraints the simulation is simpler and equally fast; present the factorial method as the scalable answer if asked to handle n up to 1e6. Pitfalls: reducing num modulo p before multiplying (values up to 500500 fit easily, but keep 64-bit intermediates), and forgetting that JavaScript numbers stay exact below 2⁵³ so modular multiplication with % is safe there. Follow-up: F(n) for n up to 1e7 (factorial-table approach becomes necessary), or products of blocks.
